sentences.text: Revenue compounded at 3.3% a year from $65.1 billion in FY2017 to $87.0 billion in FY2026 [F1][F10][F201], a steady climb rather than a step change.
The window's two big breaks are FY2019, when operating margin fell 11.9pp to 8.1% [F23][D109], and FY2020, when it rebounded 14.0pp to 22.1% [F24][D160].

The FY2019 collapse was an $8.3 billion impairment charge, including $6.8 billion of Shave Care goodwill, driven by currency devaluations, decelerating category growth and tougher US competition [X109][X112][P62].

FY2020's rebound was largely that base-period charge reversing: $8.3 billion of the $10.2 billion operating-income increase came from the prior-year impairment, with the rest from higher sales and gross margin [P71].
Since FY2020 the top line has grown 2.0% a year over the last three years [D664], and FY2026's 3.3% growth came from 2% foreign exchange and 1% pricing with volume and mix flat [D457][P26].
The US was the growth engine for most of the window, contributing 4.0pp of FY2020's 4.8% growth [D518][D147] and 2.7pp of FY2023's 2.3% [D527][D302], but only 0.1pp of FY2026's 3.3% [D536][D457].
In FY2026 the swing came from Non-US, which grew 6.1% and contributed 3.1pp, while the US grew 0.2% [D510][D511][D535].

Fabric & Home Care remains the largest segment at 34.8% of revenue, contributing 0.8pp of FY2026 growth on 2.4% segment growth [D541][D543][D542], with the filing citing favorable foreign exchange of 1% and pricing of 1% [P12].
Beauty contributed 1.3pp on 7.1% growth [D603][D602], and Health Care 0.5pp on 3.8% growth [D617][D616], while Baby, Feminine & Family Care added only 0.2pp [D564].
Profit has not kept pace with revenue lately: operating income fell 3.4% in FY2026 against 3.3% revenue growth [D458][D457], an incremental margin of -25.6% [D481].
Per-share growth has run slightly ahead of net income because the diluted count fell 1.3% in FY2026 [D476]: diluted EPS rose 1.7% against 0.5% net income growth [D461][D459].
FY2026 operating margin of 22.7% [F30] sits just above the window median of 22.1% [D648] and below the FY2025 high of 24.3% [D647], with the FY2019 low of 8.1% distorted by the impairment [D646].
The 1.6pp FY2026 decline [D470] came from a 1.0pp hit from cost of revenue and 0.6pp from SG&A [D483][D485], which the filing attributes to lower gross margin and higher marketing spending [P25].
Gross margin fell on unfavorable category mix, partly offset by lower commodity costs and productivity savings, while SG&A rose on marketing spending [P5].

Below the line, other income of $1.1 billion [X108] and a 20.8% tax rate [D443] held net margin at 18.4% [F50], a 0.5pp decline from FY2025 [D471], far smaller than the 1.6pp operating-margin drop [D470].
The other-income swing was driven by the prior-year Argentina translation charge and the current-year Glad joint-venture dissolution gain [P24].
Operating cash flow of $19.6 billion was 1.22x net income in FY2026 [F80][D444], and free cash flow of $15.1 billion was 0.94x net income [F100][D445], above the 0.87x peer median [D679].
Free-cash-flow margin of 17.4% [D441] is in line with the 17.2% window median [D654] but below the 20.5% FY2021 high [D653].

Operating cash flow rose 9.8% [D462] as net earnings plus non-cash items generated about $19.5 billion; inventories consumed $641 million on higher safety stock and new products, and payables generated $919 million [P3].
Capital intensity is rising: capex of $4.4 billion was 5.1% of revenue and 1.40x D&A [F90][D440][D446], the highest capex-to-D&A ratio in the window.
The company runs net debt of $24.2 billion, or 27.8% of revenue [D450][D451], with $9.9 billion of cash against $34.1 billion of total debt [F140][D449].
That leverage ranks at the 33rd percentile of six staples peers, whose median net cash is -1.0% of revenue [D676][D677], so P&G carries more debt than most of the group.
The current ratio is 0.68x [F180], below the 0.72x window median [D663], reflecting a working-capital deficit of $12.5 billion [F170].
Free cash flow funded $5.0 billion of buybacks and $10.2 billion of dividends in FY2026 [X134][X144], 100.7% of free cash flow [D453], and the diluted count fell 1.3% [D476].
Return on average equity of 30.1% [D456] trails the peer median of 44.4% [D681], a function of the large equity base rather than weak profitability.
The current ratio has been below 1.0x all window and stands at 0.68x in FY2026 [F180][R1], a structural feature of negative working capital rather than a new stress.
With $19.6 billion of annual operating cash flow [F80], the sub-1.0x ratio is a low-severity liquidity signal, not a solvency concern.
Buybacks plus dividends exceeded free cash flow in FY2025 and FY2026, at 116.6% and 100.7% respectively [D402][D453][R2].
Payout above free cash flow for two years, funded partly by debt, leaves less room if capex keeps climbing from 5.1% of revenue [D440].

Whether operating margin recovers toward the FY2025 high of 24.3% [D647] or stays near the 22.1% median [D648]; the FY2027 10-K's segment discussion will show if the gross-margin and marketing drag persists.
Whether free-cash-flow margin holds above the 17.2% median [D654] as capex runs at 5.1% of revenue [D440]; a move back toward the 20.5% FY2021 high [D653] would confirm the cash trend.
Whether buybacks plus dividends fall back below the FY2026 level of 100.7% of free cash flow [D453], which would reverse the FY2025-FY2026 overdistribution.
Whether Non-US growth of 6.1% [D510] persists or reverts, given the US grew only 0.2% in FY2026 [D535].
